a: The church of God that lives as a resident alien in Smyrna
t: A letter from Smyrna, and its title
p: The account is a letter from Polycarp's church. The title above it differs in every manuscript.
b: Lake: an 'obviously genuine and contemporary account of the martyrdom of Polycarp, in the form of a letter from the Church of Smyrna to the Church of Philomelium'. The greeting uses 'lives as a resident alien' (paroikousa), as 1 Clement 1:0 and Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0 do (see the note there), from 1 Peter's picture of Christians as foreigners on earth (1 Peter 1:17; 2:11). Lake prints a title above the greeting, 'The Martyrdom of the holy Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna', and notes that it 'has no special support. Each MS. gives its own title and though there is a general resemblance no two are the same.'
r: 1 Peter 1:17; 1 Peter 2:11; Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0; 20:1

a: Philomelium
p: The church that asked for the account, and the churches it was to pass it on to.
b: Philomelium had asked for a full report (20:1: 'You asked for a fuller account'), and Smyrna sends it with a request to 'send the letter on to the brothers farther away' (20:1). So the letter is written for one church and, through it, for 'all the communities ... in every place'. Eusebius gives the opening greeting in his Church History 4.15.3. He introduces the letter as sent 'to the communities in each place' (tais kata topon paroikiais, 4.15.2, in the Greek of Lake's Loeb edition); the NPNF English has instead 'to the parishes in Pontus'.

a: communities
p: Greek paroikiai, 'resident-alien settlements', the word that became 'parish'.
b: The noun paroikia belongs with the verb 'lives as a resident alien'. Each local church is a settlement of foreigners whose home is in heaven. The Latin form paroecia later became the English 'parish'. Lake renders 'sojournings'.

a: holy and catholic church
p: Lake counts the Martyrdom among the earliest clear examples of 'catholic' for the worldwide church.
b: Greek katholikē, 'according to the whole', 'universal'. Here and in 8:1 and 19:2 it means the whole church spread through the world. It is not yet the name of one communion, so the Plain English Translation writes it lowercase. Lake's footnote at 16:2: 'If the reading "Catholic" be right, this and the instance on p. 322 [8:1] are the earliest clear examples of this use of the word (but cf. Ignatius, Smyrn. viii.)'. Ignatius had written: 'wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church' (To the Smyrnaeans 8, ANF). Eusebius's copy of the greeting reads 'the holy catholic church' without 'and' (variant). On 16:2 see the variant there.
orig: τῆς ἁγίας καὶ καθολικῆς ἐκκλησίας (tēs hagias kai katholikēs ekklēsias)

a: may they be multiplied
p: 'Mercy, peace and love ... multiplied': the greeting of Jude 2.
b: Lake's margin gives Jude 2: "Mercy to you, and peace, and love: may they be multiplied" (Jude 2). The same three gifts, in the same order, open the Martyrdom.

a: martyred
p: Greek martys means 'witness'. In this letter it means one who dies for the faith.
b: The Martyrdom uses martyreō, martys, martyria and martyrion again and again, and nearly always for dying for Christ, so the Plain English Translation has 'martyr', 'be martyred' and 'martyrdom'. The root sense is 'witness', as in Acts 22:20 ('Stephen, your witness') and Revelation 2:13 ('Antipas, my witness'). Lake's footnote: 'It is not clear whether μαρτυρία and μαρτύριον ought to be translated "martyrdom" or "witness": there is an untranslateable play on the words.' The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that 'it was only by degrees, in the course of the first age of the Church, that the term martyr came to be exclusively applied to those who had died for the faith'.

a: set a seal, as it were, on the persecution
p: Polycarp was the last to die, and his death closed the persecution like a seal on a document.
b: Greek episphragisas, 'sealing'. A seal finished and confirmed a letter or will. Lake: 'He was the last to suffer and thus might be regarded as being the seal to the "witness" or "testimony" (μαρτύριον) of the Church.' Polycarp's death, as the letter tells it, both confirmed the witness of the others and ended the attacks (compare 19:1, 'the twelfth').

a: a martyrdom in line with the gospel
p: The writer tells Polycarp's death to match Jesus' passion. How much is history and how much pattern is debated.
b: The phrase to kata to euangelion martyrion sets the theme: Polycarp waits to be handed over (1:2), is betrayed by his own household (6:2), is hunted by a man named Herod (6:2), says 'May God's will be done' (7:1), rides into the city on a donkey (8:1). Lake's footnote at 6:2: 'The writer desires to bring out the points of resemblance to the Passion of Christ. The coincidences are remarkable, but none are in themselves at all improbable.' Bart Ehrman reads the same list the other way: these 'coincidences' are 'literary touches, not historical recollections', part of his case that the account 'was written decades later, by someone who wanted his readers to think he was an eyewitness' (his blog, 2023, from Forgery and Counterforgery, 2013). The likenesses themselves are in the text; whether they were noticed in real events or shaped the telling is where Lake and Ehrman part.

a: he waited to be handed over, as the Lord also did
p: Polycarp did not give himself up; he waited until he was handed over, as Jesus was.
b: The verb paradidōmi, 'hand over', is the Gospels' word for what happened to Jesus: "the Son of Man is being handed over to be crucified" (Matthew 26:2). The letter's point comes in 4:1: those who 'turn themselves in' are not praised. Polycarp waited; his arrest came from others. The model is Jesus, and through Polycarp the readers are to become 'his imitators', as Paul wrote, "Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ" (1 Corinthians 11:1).

a: keeping an eye not only on what concerns ourselves but also on what concerns our neighbors
p: Lake's margin: the line comes from Philippians 2:4, in a form of its own.
b: Paul: "Do not each keep an eye on your own concerns, but each on other people's too" (Philippians 2:4). The Martyrdom's Greek, mē monon skopountes to kath' heautous, alla kai to kata tous pelas, uses Paul's verb skopeō but says 'neighbors'. Polycarp's slowness to die, as the letter tells it, was for the sake of others: he prayed for the churches (5:1) and stayed until God's hour came.

a: by the will of God
t: Only by the will of God
p: A true martyrdom is one God chooses, not one a person seeks.
b: Greek kata to thelēma tou theou. 'Blessed and noble' are the martyrdoms that come by God's will, 'for we must be all the more reverent and give God the power over everything'. This prepares for Quintus (4:1), who rushed forward on his own and failed. Germanicus (3:1) will be the good example and Quintus (4:1) the bad.

a: their love for their Master
p: Greek philodespoton: 'master-loving', the loyalty of a good slave to his owner.
b: The word joins philos, 'loving', and despotēs, 'master', the word for the owner of slaves and, of God or Christ, 'Master' (2 Peter 2:1; Jude 4). The martyrs are slaves who love their Master; Polycarp himself will say, 'For eighty-six years I have been his slave' (9:3).

a: Some were so torn by whips
p: The martyrs were flogged until their veins showed. Eusebius repeats this in his summary.
b: Greek mastixin ... kataxanthentes, 'carded with whips', the word for combing wool. Eusebius, summarizing chapters 2-4, says the onlookers 'were struck with amazement when they saw them lacerated with scourges even to the innermost veins and arteries' (Church History 4.15.4, NPNF). The Plain English Translation gives the details as the letter does, adding nothing.

a: were away from the flesh
p: Paul hoped 'to be away from the body and at home with the Lord'.
b: Greek tēs sarkos apedēmoun, 'they were abroad from the flesh'. Paul used the same verb: "we would much prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). The letter says this as a way of explaining the martyrs' silence under pain, 'or rather', it corrects itself, the Lord was standing beside them.

a: the Lord was standing beside them and talking with them
p: As the Lord stood by Paul in court, and Stephen saw Jesus standing.
b: Paul wrote of his trial: "Yet the Lord was there beside me and made me strong" (2 Timothy 4:17). Stephen, dying, saw 'the Son of Man standing at God's right hand' (Acts 7:56). The martyrs' calm, the letter says, came from the Lord's presence.

a: buying eternal life at the price of a single hour
p: Greek exagorazomenoi: 'buying out'. One hour of pain bought eternal life.
b: The verb exagorazō means 'buy out, redeem' (Galatians 4:5; Ephesians 5:16). Here the martyrs pay with one hour of suffering and gain 'eternal life'. Most Greek manuscripts have 'eternal punishment' instead, which would mean buying their way out of it (see the variant). The short hour of pain against the endless fire returns in Polycarp's answer: 'a fire that burns for an hour' (11:2).

a: The fire of their savage torturers felt cold to them
p: Like the three young men in the furnace (Daniel 3), as the martyrs felt it.
b: The letter says the fire was 'cold' to them because they saw a worse fire to escape. The picture recalls Daniel 3, where "The fire had had no power over their bodies" (Daniel 3:27). The 'fire that is eternal and never put out' is Jesus' language: "the fire is never put out" (Mark 9:48), "the eternal fire" (Matthew 25:41). Polycarp's own fire will not burn him at all (15:2).

a: which no ear has heard and no eye has seen, and which have not come up into a human heart
p: 1 Corinthians 2:9, with ear and eye in the other order.
b: Paul: "What no eye has seen and no ear has heard, and what has not come up into a human heart, all that God has prepared for those who love him" (1 Corinthians 2:9). Lake's margin gives this verse, with Isaiah 64:4. The Martyrdom's Greek has ear before eye and adds that the Lord was showing these things to the martyrs already.

a: they were no longer human beings but already angels
p: The martyrs at death are called angels. Lake connects this with the Shepherd of Hermas, where the righteous pass on with the angels.
b: Lake's footnote: 'This passage, combined with Hermas Vis. II. ii. 7 and Sim. IX. xxv. 2, shows that the identification of the dead with angels existed in the second century in Christian circles.' Those two places are Shepherd of Hermas 6:7 and 102:2, and they say only that the righteous will have their passing with the angels: 'so that your passing may be with the holy angels' (Shepherd of Hermas 6:7), and 'people like this pass in with the angels' (Shepherd of Hermas 102:2). The identification is Lake's inference. Compared with the Bible: this goes beyond the 66 books. Jesus said the risen 'are like God's angels in heaven' (Matthew 22:30), likeness, not identity, and Hebrews distinguishes 'the spirits of righteous people made perfect' from the angels (Hebrews 12:22-23). The letter's line is praise in a strong figure, read by most churches as such.
r: Matthew 22:30; Hebrews 12:22-23; Luke 20:36; Shepherd of Hermas 6:7; Shepherd of Hermas 102:2

a: They were laid on trumpet shells
p: Greek kērykas: LSJ gives 'trumpet-shell', the shell of a sea snail, as a second sense of kēryx.
b: The noun kēryx usually means 'herald' (as in 12:1); LSJ gives a second sense, 'trumpet-shell', a kind of sea snail's shell. The martyrs were made to lie on these. The Greek has no word for 'sharp': Lake renders 'stretched on sharp shells', and Eusebius's summary adds 'certain pointed spits' (Church History 4.15.4, NPNF; Greek oxeis obeliskous).

a: the tyrant
p: The proconsul, called a tyrant, behind whom the letter sees the devil.
b: Greek ho tyrannos, a ruler who rules by force. The letter means the proconsul who judged the martyrs (3:1; 9:2), and at once names the power behind him: 'the devil was scheming many things against them'. 4 Maccabees calls King Antiochus 'the tyrant' in its story of the Jewish martyrs (4 Maccabees 5:1: 'The tyrant Antiochus took his seat').

a: the most noble Germanicus
p: A young martyr who faced the beast boldly. He is known only from this letter and Eusebius's summary.
b: Eusebius: 'the most noble Germanicus especially distinguished himself', and the proconsul 'urged his youth' and begged him, 'as he was very young and vigorous, to take compassion on himself' (Church History 4.15.5, NPNF). The Greek ethēriomachēsen, 'fought the beasts', is the verb Paul used figuratively: 'I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus' (1 Corinthians 15:32).

a: the proconsul
p: The Roman governor of the province of Asia, sitting as judge in Smyrna.
b: Greek anthypatos, as in Acts 13:7 ('the proconsul Sergius Paulus') and Acts 18:12. The province of Asia was governed by a proconsul appointed by the Senate for a year. This one is named in 21:1: Statius Quadratus. The date of his year in office is the key to dating the martyrdom (see the note at 21:1).

a: he forced the beast to come at him and dragged it onto himself
p: Germanicus did not give himself up, but once condemned he met the beast head-on.
b: The letter praises Germanicus and, in the next breath, blames Quintus (4:1). The difference is that Germanicus was arrested and condemned; he did not volunteer. Once in the arena he refused the proconsul's pity and pulled the animal toward himself, 'because he wanted to be set free sooner from their unjust and lawless life'. Ignatius had written of coaxing the beasts to devour him quickly (quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.36.8).

a: Away with the atheists!
p: Greek atheoi: those who deny the gods. The crowd called Christians atheists.
b: LSJ defines atheos as 'without God, denying the gods, esp. those recognized by the state'. Christians would not worship the city's gods or the emperor's image, so to their neighbors they were 'atheists'. The cry Aire, 'take away!', is the crowd's cry against Jesus: "Away with him! Away! Crucify him!" (John 19:15). In 9:2 the proconsul asks Polycarp to shout it himself, and Polycarp does, pointing at the crowd.

a: a Phrygian who had come from Phrygia not long before
p: A newcomer from Phrygia, the inland region east of Smyrna, who urged others to give themselves up and then gave way.
b: The letter names his origin twice, 'a Phrygian ... from Phrygia', and adds that he had come 'not long before'. Eusebius tells the story in his own words and draws the lesson: 'it is not right for such persons rashly and recklessly to expose themselves to danger' (Church History 4.15.7-8, NPNF). The text says no more about who Quintus was.

a: we give no praise to people who turn themselves in, because that is not what the gospel teaches
p: The letter's rule: wait to be arrested, as Polycarp did, and do not volunteer.
b: Lake's margin gives Matthew 10:23: "When they hunt you down in this town, escape to the next" (Matthew 10:23). The Catholic Encyclopedia says 'the orthodox were not permitted to seek martyrdom', notes that Tertullian and Eusebius sometimes approved Christians who gave themselves up, and cites Gregory of Nazianzus: 'it is mere rashness to seek death, but it is cowardly to refuse it'. It also uses Quintus as 'a warning of what might happen to the over-zealous'.

a: swearing the oath and offering sacrifice
p: To go free, an accused Christian had to swear by the emperor and offer sacrifice.
b: Quintus did what Polycarp later refuses: he swore and sacrificed. The oath was 'by the fortune of Caesar' (9:2), and the sacrifice was offered to the gods or the emperor (8:2). Doing these showed loyalty to the state's gods; Christians who refused were taken to be 'atheists' (3:2).

a: urged him to slip away
p: Polycarp left the city at his friends' urging, as Matthew 10:23 allows.
b: Greek hypexelthein, 'to go out quietly'. Polycarp first wanted to stay; he left because 'most of them' urged it. Eusebius: he 'determined to remain in the city. But being persuaded by his friends ... he went out to a farm not far distant' (Church History 4.15.9, NPNF). The letter's point, with 4:1, is that a Christian should neither seek death nor deny Christ when it comes.

a: pray for everyone and for the churches all over the world
p: Polycarp's last days were given to prayer for others, as Jesus prayed for his disciples before his arrest.
b: Compare Jesus' prayer for his disciples before his arrest in John 17 ('I am asking you to keep them safe from the evil one', John 17:15). The letter adds 'as he always did': prayer for the churches was his habit, not only his farewell. In 8:1 he remembers 'the whole catholic church throughout the world'.

a: he had a vision and saw his pillow being burned up by fire
p: A vision three days before his arrest, which he read as a sign of his death by fire.
b: Greek en optasia, 'in a vision', the same word as in 12:3 ('the vision of his pillow'). The pillow under his head, burning, meant the death he would die: 'I must be burned alive.' The letter returns to it in 12:3: the crowd's cry for fire happened because 'the vision of his pillow had to be fulfilled'. Some of the Greek manuscripts spell the verb 'burned' differently (Lake: kaēnai m, kauthēnai bpsv); the meaning is the same. The letter presents the vision as a true prophecy (12:3; 16:2).

a: two slave boys
p: Greek paidaria: 'little boys', a common word for young slaves.
b: Lake: 'Literally "children," but constantly used for slaves'. The Plain English Translation has 'slave boys' here and in 7:1, and keeps 'servant' for the different use of pais in Polycarp's prayer (14:1). One of them 'confessed under torture', that is, told where Polycarp was.

a: the ones who betrayed him belonged to his own household
p: Lake's margin: Matthew 10:36.
b: "Those in a man's own house will be his enemies" (Matthew 10:36). The Greek oikeioi means members of his household, here the slave boys or others of the farm. The writer sets them beside Judas: 'those who betrayed him might suffer the punishment of Judas himself' (compare Matthew 27:5).

a: the police captain
p: Greek eirēnarchos, 'peace-ruler': a local officer charged with keeping order and arresting suspects.
b: Lake renders 'police captain'. This one, Herod, and his father Nicetes (8:2) are leading men of Smyrna. Nothing in the text says whether they were Jews or Gentiles.

a: who had been given the very same name, for he was called Herod
p: The letter notes that Polycarp's captor bore the name of the Herod of Jesus' passion.
b: Greek ho keklērōmenos to auto onoma, 'allotted the same name'. In Luke, Herod Antipas questions and mocks Jesus (Luke 23:7-12; compare Acts 4:27, 'Herod and Pontius Pilate'). The letter sees the name as part of God's design, and plays on klēros, 'lot': Herod was 'allotted' the name, and Polycarp would 'fulfill his own lot' as a sharer with Christ. Lake: 'The coincidences are remarkable, but none are in themselves at all improbable.'

a: on the Day of Preparation
p: Greek paraskeuē, the day before the Sabbath, the day of Jesus' death.
b: Lake: 'paraskeuē is literally Preparation (i.e. for the Sabbath) and has always been used in the Greek Church for Friday.' Mark 15:42: 'it was the Day of Preparation, which is the day before the Sabbath'. Polycarp is arrested on a Friday evening and dies the next day, on 'a great Sabbath' (8:1; 21:1).

a: as if they were rushing out against a bandit
p: Lake's margin: Matthew 26:55, Jesus' words at his arrest.
b: "Am I a bandit, that you come out with swords and clubs to take me?" (Matthew 26:55). The Greek hōs epi lēstēn is the same phrase. Lake: '"robber" is the traditional translation: but "brigand" is nearer the real meaning.' The armed men, diōgmitai ('pursuers', a kind of police) and horsemen, are sent against an old man (7:2).

a: May God's will be done
p: Lake's margin: Acts 21:14 and Matthew 6:10.
b: When Paul would not be talked out of going to Jerusalem, his friends said: "May the Lord's will be done" (Acts 21:14). The Lord's Prayer has "May your will be done" (Matthew 6:10), and in Gethsemane Jesus prayed "may your will be done" (Matthew 26:42). Eusebius has the words too: 'The will of God be done' (Church History 4.15.12, NPNF).

a: he gave orders for food and drink to be set before them
p: Polycarp acts as host to the men who came to arrest him.
b: He feeds them 'as much as they wanted' and asks only an hour to pray. Compare the Last Supper (Matthew 26:17-29). The Gospel parallel for the hour is Gethsemane: "Were you not strong enough to keep awake with me for one hour?" (Matthew 26:40). The kindness also fits Jesus' command to do good to enemies (Romans 12:20).

a: for two hours he could not stop
p: The prayer moved even the arresting party.
b: Eusebius's summary: 'he stood up and prayed, being full of the grace of the Lord, so that those who were present and heard him praying were amazed, and many of them now repented that such a venerable and godly old man was about to be put to death' (Church History 4.15.14, NPNF). The letter's 'many were sorry' is the verb metanoeō, 'repent', which returns in the proconsul's demand (9:2; 11:1).

a: the whole catholic church throughout the world
p: Here 'catholic' plainly means worldwide: 'throughout the world'.
b: Greek pasēs tēs kata tēn oikoumenēn katholikēs ekklēsias. The words 'throughout the world' show what 'catholic' means: the church in every place, as in the greeting (1:0) and 19:2. Lake's footnote at 16:2 counts this among the earliest clear examples of the word in this sense. Eusebius quotes it: 'the whole Catholic Church throughout the world' (Church History 4.15.15, NPNF).
orig: τῆς κατὰ τὴν οἰκουμένην καθολικῆς ἐκκλησίας

a: They sat him on a donkey and brought him into the city
t: Into the city on a donkey
p: The old man is brought into Smyrna on a donkey, as Jesus entered Jerusalem.
b: John 12:14: 'Jesus found a little donkey and sat on it'. The letter does not draw out this likeness itself; it is one of the details that match the passion, which 1:1 says the whole account shows (see the note at 1:1).

a: It was a great Sabbath
p: John calls the Sabbath after Jesus' death 'a great day'. Which Sabbath Smyrna's 'great Sabbath' was is debated.
b: Greek sabbatou megalou, as again in 21:1. John 19:31: 'that Sabbath was a great day'. Lake's footnote: 'This may have been the Jewish feast Purim ... or else the Sabbath in the Passover week'. His introduction reports C. H. Turner's argument for Purim, 22 February 156, and E. Schwartz's for 'the Sabbath after the Passover' by Smyrna's local Jewish reckoning, reaching the same day by another route. The phrase shows that the Christians of Smyrna marked time by the Jewish calendar around them.

a: Lord Caesar
p: Greek Kyrios Kaisar has no verb: a title, as Lake and Eusebius read it. More than that, the text leaves open.
b: The Greek Kyrios Kaisar has no verb. Lake renders it 'Lord Caesar', and Eusebius quotes the same two words (kyrios Kaisar, Church History 4.15.15; NPNF 'Lord Cæsar'), so the Plain English Translation gives it as a title. The text leaves open whether the words meant more than a courtesy. They have the shape of the Christian confession "Jesus is Lord" (1 Corinthians 12:3), and the letter will set Caesar against Polycarp's 'King' (9:3), but it does not call the words a confession. Whether a Christian could call the emperor 'lord' at all was argued a generation later. Tertullian wrote that Augustus 'would not even have the title Lord; for that, too, is a name of Deity', and that he himself was 'willing to give the emperor this designation, but in the common acceptation of the word, and when I am not forced to call him Lord as in God's place' (Apology 34, ANF). What Herod and Nicetes asked was the words together with sacrifice (8:2), and Polycarp refused both.

a: their carriage
p: Lake: the karoucha was the Latin carruca, a closed carriage for ladies and high officials.
b: Lake's footnote: 'karoucha (cf. Corpus Inscr. Lat. iii. p. 835) is the Latin "carucca," a closed carriage used by ladies and high officials.' Eusebius's Greek has the common word ochēma, 'carriage', instead of the Latin loanword (Church History 4.15.15). Herod and Nicetes give the old man a seat of honor and talk to him privately, before turning rough when he refuses (8:3).

a: his father Nicetes
p: Nicetes is called the brother of Alce (17:2). Ignatius had greeted an Alce at Smyrna.
b: The letter names Nicetes here and in 17:2, where he is 'Herod's father and the brother of Alce'. Ignatius, writing to Smyrna some decades earlier, greeted 'Alce, my well-beloved' (To the Smyrnaeans 13; To Polycarp 8, ANF). If this is the same woman, a Christian of Smyrna had a brother and nephew among the officials who arrested Polycarp. The texts do not say that they are the same person.

a: he scraped his shin as he got down from the carriage
p: Polycarp scrapes his shin and walks on.
b: Hurried down from the carriage, Polycarp scrapes his shin and walks on 'as if nothing had happened'. Eusebius repeats it (Church History 4.15.16, NPNF: 'he lacerated his shin').

a: a voice came from heaven
p: Only the Christians present heard it. Its words are God's charge to Joshua in the Greek Bible.
b: Greek Ischye, Polykarpe, kai andrizou. Lake's margin gives Joshua 1:6, where the Greek has ischye kai andrizou for the Hebrew that the site renders "Be strong and bold" (Joshua 1:6). The Plain English Translation renders andrizou 'show courage', as the site's 1 Corinthians 16:13 renders the same verb. Like the voice at Jesus' baptism and in John 12:28, it came from heaven; 'no one saw who spoke, but those of our people who were there heard the voice'. Eusebius has it too (Church History 4.15.17).

a: Swear by the fortune of Caesar
p: Greek tychē, 'fortune', for the Latin fortuna (Lake). Christians refused to swear by it.
b: Lake's footnote: 'The customary Greek for the oath "per genium" (or sometimes "fortunam", hence τύχην) Caesaris which Christians rejected. Per salutem Caesaris (σωτηρίαν) they accepted. (Cf Tertullian Apol. 32.)' Tertullian wrote: 'though we decline to swear by the genii of the Cæsars, we swear by their safety', because the 'genii' were, to him, demons (Apology 32, ANF). Whether Christians may take oaths at all is the question of the site's cards at Matthew 5 and in the Histories of Tacitus 4.
orig: Ὄμοσον τὴν Καίσαρος τύχην (Omoson tēn Kaisaros tychēn)

a: looked up to heaven and said, "Away with the atheists!"
p: Polycarp says the words he is told to say. How he means them, the letter shows only by his gestures.
b: The proconsul wants Polycarp to shout the crowd's slogan against the Christians (3:2). Polycarp says the very words, and the letter tells how: he looks with a stern face at 'the whole crowd of lawless Gentiles', waves his hand at them, groans and looks up to heaven. It does not explain. The gestures suggest that he turns the cry back on the crowd, as people who do not know God (compare Ephesians 2:12); on another reading he simply says what he was told, in words that are true in his own sense. Eusebius's Greek lacks 'lawless Gentiles': in his copy Polycarp looks at 'the whole crowd in the stadium' (Church History 4.15.19; see the variant).

a: For eighty-six years I have been his slave
p: The most famous words of the account, and a clue to Polycarp's age.
b: Greek Ogdoēkonta kai hex etē douleuō autō, 'eighty-six years I serve him', the present tense of lifelong service. Lake's footnote: 'He was therefore probably a Christian born, unless we ascribe to him a quite improbable age.' So Lake takes the eighty-six years most likely as his whole life, and leaves the other reading open: years counted from his conversion, which would make him older still. Lake's introduction to Polycarp's letter (vol. 1) puts his death 'at the age of eighty-six'. If he died in 155 or 156, he was born about AD 69-70. The verb douleuō is a slave's service, and the Plain English Translation keeps 'slave', as for doulos elsewhere.
orig: Ὀγδοήκοντα καὶ ἓξ ἔτη δουλεύω αὐτῷ

a: my King, the one who saved me
p: Lake: basileus here answers to the emperor's title. Polycarp's King is Christ.
b: Lake's footnote: 'basileus represents "imperator" not "rex," and though it can hardly be translated "Emperor," the antithesis to Caesar is clearly implied.' The proconsul offers Caesar's fortune; Polycarp names his own King. The letter ends the same way: Polycarp died 'while Jesus Christ was reigning as King forever' (21:1).
orig: τὸν βασιλέα μου τὸν σώσαντά με

a: I am a Christian
p: Confessing the name was enough for a death sentence.
b: Greek Christianos eimi. The proconsul's herald announces exactly this as the charge: 'Polycarp has confessed that he is a Christian' (12:1). The name was first used at Antioch (Acts 11:26), and 1 Peter 4:16 speaks of suffering 'for being a Christian'. Polycarp offers to explain the faith if given a day to do it, a request the proconsul ignores.

a: rulers and authorities appointed by God
p: Lake's margin: Romans 13:1 and 1 Peter 2:13.
b: Paul: the authorities 'have been set in their places by God' (Romans 13:1), with the same verb tassō as the Martyrdom's tetagmenais. Peter: 'Submit to the king as the one ranked highest' (1 Peter 2:13). Polycarp grants the proconsul honor, 'as long as it does us no harm', that is, short of denying Christ. He will reason with the governor, but not with the crowd. How far Christians owe obedience to the state is the subject of the topic Church and state.

a: a repentance from better to worse is out of the question
p: The proconsul demands that Polycarp 'repent'; Polycarp turns the word back.
b: Greek metanoia, 'change of mind, repentance'. The proconsul has said 'Repent' (9:2) and now 'unless you repent'. Polycarp answers that a change from better to worse is no repentance at all, but 'it is good to turn from what is cruel to what is right', which is what the proconsul ought to do.
orig: ἀμετάθετος γὰρ ἡμῖν ἡ ἀπὸ τῶν κρειττόνων ἐπὶ τὰ χείρω μετάνοια

a: the fire of the coming judgment and eternal punishment
p: The proconsul's fire lasts an hour; the fire of judgment does not end.
b: Polycarp sets 'a fire that burns for an hour and is soon put out' against 'the fire ... which is kept for the ungodly'. Jesus: 'Go away from me ... into the eternal fire made ready for the devil and his angels' (Matthew 25:41); 'the fire is never put out' (Mark 9:48). 2 Peter 3:7 speaks of the world 'kept for fire on the day of judgment'.

a: his face was full of grace
p: Like Stephen's face before the council.
b: At his trial Stephen's face 'looked like an angel's face' (Acts 6:15). The letter describes Polycarp in the same way: courage, joy and grace on his face, so that it is the judge who is shaken. Eusebius quotes it (Church History 4.15.25).

a: the whole crowd of Gentiles and Jews who lived in Smyrna
t: The Jews of Smyrna in the account
p: The letter blames Smyrna's Jews four times.
b: The letter names the Jews here, gathering wood 'as is their habit' (13:1), urging that the body be withheld (17:2) and quarreling at the pyre (18:1). Revelation had already spoken of 'the slander that comes from those who say they are Jews and are not' at Smyrna (Revelation 2:9). The letter gives no way to check its report. The crowd's cry for death also follows the passion pattern the letter points to (1:1; compare John 19:12-16). Eusebius keeps these lines (Church History 4.15.26, 29, 41-43). The site's topic on Christian anti-Judaism discusses how such texts were later used.

a: the teacher of Asia, the father of the Christians, the destroyer of our gods
t: What the crowd said of him
p: The pagan crowd's charges show Polycarp's standing and why they feared him.
b: To the crowd he is 'the teacher of Asia', a leader known across the province, and the man who 'teaches many not to sacrifice or to worship'. Compare the silversmiths of Ephesus, whose trade Paul's preaching threatened (Acts 19:24-27). The OCA's life of Polycarp repeats the titles 'the father of all the Christians' and 'the seducer of all Asia'.

a: Philip the Asiarch
p: LSJ: an Asiarch was a priest of the imperial cult in the province of Asia. 21:1 names a Philip as 'high priest'.
b: Greek Asiarchēs. LSJ defines it as 'priest of the Imperial cult in the province of Asia' and cites Acts 19:31, where the site has 'Some of the Asiarchs too'. 21:1 names 'Philip of Tralles' as 'high priest'; taking the two as one man is an inference from the name and the two titles, which the letter does not state. Philip said he could not set a lion loose, 'since he had brought the animal hunts to a close' (Lake's footnote: the word for the games, kynēgesia, is 'Literally "hunting," the Latin "venatio"', the beast-hunts of the arena).

a: as a prophet
p: Greek prophētikōs: Polycarp's word about the fire was a prophecy.
b: The letter calls Polycarp 'an apostolic and prophetic teacher' (16:2) and says 'every word that came from his mouth has been fulfilled'. The vision of 5:2 is its proof. Like Agabus's warning to Paul (Acts 21:10-11), the prophecy does not change the outcome; it shows that God knew it.

a: with the Jews especially eager to help with this, as is their habit
p: The harshest line about the Jews in the letter.
b: The writer says the Jews helped gather fuel 'especially eager ... as is their habit'. Eusebius quotes it: 'the Jews being especially zealous in the work, as is their wont' (Church History 4.15.29, NPNF). Revelation 2:9 already speaks of conflict at Smyrna. Whatever happened that day, a whole people is blamed for its 'habit'. See the note at 12:2 and the topic on Christian anti-Judaism.

a: each of the believers was always eager to be the first to touch his skin
p: Even before his death the faithful honored Polycarp by touching him.
b: Polycarp had never taken off his own sandals, because believers competed to do it for him and so to touch him. The letter explains it by 'his good way of life', for which he had been 'adorned with every good thing' even before his martyrdom; Eusebius's Greek reads instead 'even before his gray hair' (Church History 4.15.30; see the variant). Compare Acts 19:12, where cloths that had touched Paul were carried to the sick, and Acts 5:15. The same honor turns to his body and bones after his death (17:1; 18:2).

a: When they were about to nail him as well
p: Polycarp asks not to be nailed to the stake, trusting God to keep him still in the fire.
b: The men preparing the pyre were about to nail him as well. Polycarp says 'the one who lets me endure the fire will let me stay on the pyre without flinching', and they tie him instead (14:1). Eusebius gives the same (Church History 4.15.31). The nails also recall Jesus' crucifixion (John 20:25).

a: like a choice ram taken from a great flock for an offering
p: Bound, hands behind him, Polycarp is a sacrifice, like the ram God gave in Isaac's place.
b: The words gather the language of sacrifice: a 'choice ram' (krios episēmos), an 'offering', 'a whole burnt offering ... acceptable to God'. At Mount Moriah, Abraham found 'a ram ... and offered it up as a burnt offering in place of his son' (Genesis 22:13). The burnt offering was 'a soothing smell for the LORD' (Leviticus 1:9); compare the sweet scent of 15:2. Polycarp's prayer asks to be taken in 'as a sacrifice rich and acceptable' (14:2; compare Romans 12:1).

a: your beloved and blessed servant Jesus Christ
p: Greek pais can mean 'child' or 'servant'. Lake says 'Child' here; the site says 'servant', as in Acts, with a gloss giving 'child'.
b: Greek paidos sou. Lake's footnote: 'This use of pais as applied to Jesus is rare, and usually found in prayers; cf. ... Didache 9, 2, I Clement 59, 2 ... and Acts 3, 13. 26. 4, 27. 30. Here it is clearly "Child": in Acts it may mean "Servant" with reference to Is. 53'. Lake's English has 'Child' here, in 14:3 and in 20:2 ('only begotten Child'), and the NPNF English of Eusebius has 'Son' at 14:1 and 14:3 (Church History 4.15.33, 35), where Eusebius's Greek has the same word pais. The site renders it 'servant' in all these early prayers, as in Acts 3:13 ('his servant Jesus') and Acts 4:27, so the reader sees one word; Isaiah's servant songs (Isaiah 42:1; 52:13) use the same Greek. Here, with 'Father of', the sense 'child' is the nearer one, as Lake says, so a gloss at each of the three places gives it.
orig: τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ καὶ εὐλογητοῦ παιδός σου
r: Acts 3:13; Acts 4:27; Acts 4:30; Isaiah 42:1; Didache 9:2; 1 Clement 59:2

a: Lord God, the Almighty
p: The title of God in Revelation's heavenly worship.
b: Greek Kyrie ho theos ho pantokratōr, the words of Revelation 4:8 ('is the Lord God, the Almighty') and 11:17. The prayer moves from God as Father of Jesus, to God of all creation, to God of 'the righteous who live in your presence', the martyrs among them. Eusebius's Greek lacks the address: in his copy the ram is 'an acceptable whole burnt offering to God Almighty', and the prayer begins 'Father of your beloved ...' (Church History 4.15.32-33; see the variant).

a: in the cup of your Christ
p: The cup Jesus said his disciples would drink: suffering and death.
b: Jesus asked James and John: 'Can you drink the cup that I am drinking?' and told them, "The cup I am drinking, you will drink" (Mark 10:39). In Gethsemane he prayed, 'let this cup go past me' (Matthew 26:39). Polycarp thanks God for his share in that cup. Lake's footnote says one manuscript (p) and Eusebius lack 'your'; Lake's own later edition of Eusebius prints it (see the variant). In the Gospels the cup is suffering; this prayer does not name the Lord's Supper.
orig: ἐν τῷ ποτηρίῳ τοῦ Χριστοῦ σου

a: for the resurrection to eternal life, of soul and body
p: Lake's margin: John 5:29, 'a resurrection that brings life'.
b: Jesus: "Those who did good will go out to a resurrection that brings life" (John 5:29). Polycarp prays for resurrection 'of soul and body', and 'in the incorruption of the Holy Spirit' (compare 1 Corinthians 15:42, 'raised imperishable').

a: you the God who does not lie, the true God
t: The God who does not lie
p: Titus 1:2 and the 'true God' of John.
b: "The God who does not lie promised that life before the long ages of time" (Titus 1:2). God has 'prepared ... showed ... and fulfilled' this death, as the vision of the pillow (5:2) foretold it. 'True God' is the language of John 17:3 and 1 John 5:20.

a: through the eternal and heavenly high priest Jesus Christ
p: Hebrews' title for Christ, which Polycarp also used in his letter.
b: Hebrews: 'We have a great high priest, then, one who has gone right through the heavens: Jesus, the Son of God' (Hebrews 4:14). Polycarp's letter prays to 'the eternal high priest himself, God's Son Jesus Christ' (Polycarp to the Philippians 12:2, in Latin). The prayer of the dying man and the prayer of his letter share the title. Eusebius's Greek lacks 'heavenly' (Church History 4.15.35; see the variant).
r: Hebrews 4:14; Hebrews 6:20; Hebrews 7:24-26; Polycarp to the Philippians 12:2

a: with him and the Holy Spirit
t: Glory with the Son and the Spirit
p: Glory to the Father, through the Son, 'with him and the Holy Spirit'; Eusebius's copy has 'with him, in the Holy Spirit'.
b: The prayer ends: 'through him be glory to you, with him and the Holy Spirit, both now and for the ages to come'. In Lake's text Father, Son and Spirit are named together in one act of praise, as in Matthew 28:19 and 2 Corinthians 13:14. Eusebius's Greek reads syn autō en pneumati hagiō, 'with him, in the Holy Spirit' (Church History 4.15.35; NPNF 'through whom, with him, in the Holy Spirit'), where Lake prints syn autō kai pneumati hagiō: in Eusebius's copy the Spirit is the one in whom glory is given, not a third named beside the Son (see the variant). Both forms name all three. Doxologies with 'the Father and the Holy Spirit' close the later notes (22:1; 22:3).

a: we saw a wonder, we to whom it was given to see
p: The writers claim to have seen it themselves.
b: The 'we' of 15:1 are Christians of Smyrna who were in the crowd and 'were kept safe so that we could tell the others'. Eusebius quotes it (Church History 4.15.36). Lake calls the account 'contemporary'; Bart Ehrman answers that the writer 'asserts his eyewitness authority precisely at the points that are, well, rather difficult to believe' (his blog, 2023; see the note at 1:1). What they saw, in the next verse, is a fire that would not burn the body.

a: like a sail swelling with wind on a ship
p: The flames arch over him like a vaulted room or a ship's sail filled with wind.
b: Greek kamaras eidos, 'the shape of a vault', and hōsper othonē ploiou hypo pneumatos plēroumenē. The word pneuma means both 'wind' and 'spirit'; the letter says no more. Eusebius quotes it: 'the fire presented the appearance of a vault, like the sail of a vessel filled by the wind' (Church History 4.15.37, NPNF).
orig: ὥσπερ ὀθόνη πλοίου ὑπὸ πνεύματος πληρουμένη

a: like a loaf in the oven, or like gold and silver being refined in a furnace
p: Not burning flesh but baking bread, and metal purified by fire. Eusebius's copy has only the gold and silver.
b: Gold and silver refined by fire are the Bible's picture of faith proved by trial: "I will bring the third part into the fire, and refine them the way silver is refined" (Zechariah 13:9); compare 1 Peter 1:7. Eusebius's Greek has no loaf: in his copy the body is 'not like flesh burning, but like gold and silver refined in a furnace' (Church History 4.15.37, NPNF; see the variant). The bread stands in Lake's manuscripts only. Ignatius, on his way to die, had written: 'I am God's wheat, and by the teeth of wild beasts am I ground, that I may be found pure bread' (quoted by Irenaeus in Eusebius, Church History 3.36.12, NPNF). See Claude's theory on the chapter page.

a: a scent as sweet as rising incense
p: The burnt offering's 'soothing smell', and Paul's 'sweet perfume of Christ'.
b: The sacrifice of 14:1 gives off the scent of incense. Leviticus calls the burnt offering 'a soothing smell for the LORD' (Leviticus 1:9), and Paul: "we are the sweet perfume of Christ to God" (2 Corinthians 2:15); compare Ephesians 5:2, Christ 'an offering and a sacrifice to God, a soothing smell'.

a: an executioner
p: Greek komphektōr, from Latin confector: the man who finished off beasts or victims in the arena.
b: The Greek borrows a Latin word, confector, 'one who finishes'. Lake renders 'executioner', the NPNF Eusebius 'an executioner'. He is ordered to 'drive in a dagger' (parabysai xiphidion) because the fire would not consume the body; Eusebius's Greek has xiphos, 'sword' (NPNF 'pierce him with the sword'; see the variant).

a: a dove came out
p: A miracle in the manuscripts; missing in Eusebius; a misreading according to one emendation.
b: The Greek manuscripts read 'there came out a dove and so much blood' (peristera kai plēthos haimatos). Eusebius has only 'a quantity of blood' (Church History 4.15.39, NPNF), and Lake's footnote says peristera kai is 'om. E', adding that Wordsworth emended it to peri styraka, '(round the sword-haft)'. Lake also explains the dove: 'This no doubt points to the belief that the spirit appears at death in the form of a bird. Cf. Prudentius ... (other references are also given by Lightfoot).' The Spirit came down 'like a dove' at Jesus' baptism (Matthew 3:16). See the variant entry.

a: overseer of the catholic church in Smyrna
p: Greek episkopos, the word behind 'bishop'. By now one man is the overseer of Smyrna's church.
b: The site renders episkopos 'overseer' in every book, from Philippians 1:1 ('with overseers and deacons') to this verse, so that the reader can follow the word's history without the translation deciding when 'overseer' became 'bishop', which is a point on which today's churches differ (see the cards at Philippians 1, 1 Timothy 3 and Acts 20). Here it is one man's title. The title Lake prints above the letter calls Polycarp 'overseer of Smyrna', but Lake notes that each manuscript has its own title (see the note at 1:0). Polycarp's own letter names only elders (Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0; 5:3).
r: Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:1-2; Acts 20:28; Polycarp to the Philippians 5:3

a: an apostolic and prophetic teacher
p: Polycarp is praised as a teacher in the line of the apostles and prophets.
b: Greek didaskalos apostolikos kai prophētikos. 'Apostolic' fits what Irenaeus says of him, that he 'was not only instructed by apostles' but appointed by them (Against Heresies 3.3.4); 'prophetic', what the letter has shown (5:2; 12:3). Compare Ephesians 2:20, the church 'built on the apostles and prophets'.

a: the crown of incorruption
t: The crown that does not fade
p: The victor's wreath of the games, which Paul applied to the Christian life.
b: Greek ton tēs aphtharsias stephanon. Paul: athletes compete 'to receive a crown that fades. We do it for one that never fades' (1 Corinthians 9:25). Revelation promised Smyrna's church 'the crown of life' (Revelation 2:10). The 'prize' (brabeion) is Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 9:24 and Philippians 3:14.

a: to have a share in his holy flesh
t: A share in his holy flesh
p: Greek koinōnēsai: to have fellowship with, to share in. They wanted his body, to bury and honor it.
b: The verb koinōneō is 'have a share in, have fellowship with'. The believers wanted to take Polycarp's body, 'his poor body' (sōmation), and so to keep communion with him. Lake renders 'to have fellowship with his holy flesh'. The next verses show what the officials feared and what the Christians did (17:2-18:3). Whether Christians should honor relics is the question of the site's card at 2 Kings 13.

a: or else," he said, "they will abandon the crucified one and start to worship this man
p: Nicetes argues that if the Christians get the body, they will worship Polycarp instead of Christ.
b: In Lake's text the evil one 'prompted Nicetes'; in Eusebius's Greek 'certain people' did (hypebalon goun tines, Church History 4.15.41; see the variant). Either way the letter adds that 'they said this at the prompting and urging of the Jews' (see the note at 12:2). The fear it reports is that the Christians would 'abandon the crucified one and start to worship this man'. The letter answers at once: 'we will never be able to abandon Christ ... or to worship anyone else' (17:2-3).

a: who suffered for the salvation of the whole world of those who are saved, the blameless one for sinners
p: 1 Peter 3:18: 'the one who was righteous for those who were not'.
b: Christ suffered 'for the salvation of the whole world of those who are saved'. The last words, amōmon hyper hamartōlōn, 'blameless for sinners', echo 1 Peter 3:18: "For Christ too suffered for sins, a single time, the one who was righteous for those who were not" (1 Peter 3:18). Eusebius's Greek lacks 'the blameless one for sinners' (Church History 4.15.41; see the variant), so the echo stands in Lake's manuscripts only. The phrase 'of those who are saved' limits 'the whole world', as 2 Corinthians 2:15 speaks of 'those who are being saved'.

a: For Christ we worship, because he is the Son of God. The martyrs we love
p: The letter's own line between worship of Christ and love for the martyrs.
b: Greek touton men ... proskynoumen, tous de martyras ... agapōmen. Christ is worshiped as Son of God; the martyrs are loved 'as disciples and imitators of the Lord'. The letter's words of worship are two. Proskyneō, here and in the crowd's charge (12:2), LSJ: 'make obeisance to the gods or their images, fall down and worship', and also of 'prostrating oneself before kings and superiors'. Sebesthai (17:2), what the officials fear the Christians will do for Polycarp, Middle Liddell (σέβω): 'to worship, honour'. Of the martyrs the letter uses neither, only 'love'. Later Catholic theology names the worship due to God alone latria: the Catholic Encyclopedia says relics are honored 'with a veneration which is not that of latria (divine worship)', following Thomas Aquinas. The letter itself does not use latreuō. Compared with the Bible: worship of Christ matches the New Testament (John 20:28; Hebrews 1:6), and honor for faithful leaders who have died matches Hebrews 13:7 ('imitate their faith'). What honoring the saints may include (asking their prayers, venerating images and relics) is where the churches differ; the site's cards at Acts 10, Revelation 5 and 2 Kings 13 give each tradition's view.

a: the centurion
p: A Roman officer settles the dispute by burning the body.
b: Greek ho kentyriōn, a Latin word in Greek letters, as in Mark 15:39, 44; Eusebius's Greek has the Greek word hekatontarchēs instead (Church History 4.15.43; see the variant). He places the body 'in the middle' of the fire 'as was their custom'; the letter does not say whose custom. Even so, the Christians gathered the bones (18:2).

a: his bones, worth more than costly gems and more prized than gold
p: Smyrna's Christians gathered Polycarp's bones and laid them to rest with honor.
b: Greek ta timiōtera lithōn polytelōn kai dokimōtera hyper chrysion ostā autou. The Catholic Encyclopedia quotes this line for the early Christian care of martyrs' remains: these relics 'the Christians regarded as "more valuable than gold or precious stones"' (Hassett, 'Martyr'). Its article 'Relics' (Thurston) calls this letter 'the classical instance' of the early veneration of relics, and quotes Harnack from the other side: 'Most offensive ... was the worship of relics'. Compared with the Bible: the Bible records careful burial of the faithful (Acts 8:2); Joseph's charge, "carry my bones up from here" (Genesis 50:25), which Moses kept: "Moses took Joseph's bones with him" (Exodus 13:19); and the dead man who "touched Elisha's bones" and "came to life" (2 Kings 13:21). It does not tell of a church keeping a martyr's bones where it gathers. The churches read these passages differently; the site's card at 2 Kings 13 gives each view.

a: the birthday of his martyrdom
p: Greek genethlios hēmera: the day of death, kept as a birthday into eternal life.
b: The church plans to gather each year at the tomb on the day Polycarp died and call it his 'birthday' (genethlios), the day he was born into life with God. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that 'special commemoration services of the martyrs ... were held on the anniversaries of their death'. The Catholic Encyclopedia's article 'Relics' quotes this verse with 18:2. The Orthodox Church in America keeps Polycarp's day on 23 February. Lake's note on 'fought the contest' (proēthlēkotōn): 'This is almost a technical term for martyrdom'.
orig: τὴν τοῦ μαρτυρίου αὐτοῦ ἡμέραν γενέθλιον

a: the twelfth together with those from Philadelphia
p: Polycarp was the twelfth to die; some of the others came from Philadelphia.
b: Greek syn tois apo Philadelphias dōdekatos. Eusebius: Polycarp 'suffered martyrdom in Smyrna with the eleven from Philadelphia' (Church History 4.15.45, NPNF), and this is where Eusebius's quotation ends. Philadelphia, east of Smyrna, is another of the seven churches of Revelation (Revelation 3:7-13). Of the other eleven, the letter names only Germanicus (3:1).

a: the Pilot of our bodies, and the Shepherd of the catholic church
p: Three titles for Christ, the second from seafaring.
b: Greek sōtēra tōn psychōn hēmōn kai kybernētēn tōn sōmatōn hēmōn kai poimena. A kybernētēs is a ship's pilot or helmsman (Acts 27:11), the root of 'govern'. 1 Peter calls Christ 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls' (1 Peter 2:25). Lake notes that one manuscript (m) lacks the first 'our' (see the variant). The letter's last glimpse of Polycarp is in heaven, praising God with the apostles.

a: our brother Marcion
p: The man who wrote up the account. The manuscripts give his name three ways.
b: The Moscow manuscript reads Marcion (Markiōnos), most Greek manuscripts Marcus, and the Latin Marcianus; Lake prints Marcion and notes that 'Lightfoot prefers Μαρκιανοῦ' (see the variant). Lake: 'Not of course to be identified with the famous heretic. If Marcianus be the right text, it is noteworthy that Irenaeus sent his treatise on the "The Apostolic Preaching" to a certain Marcianus. But this was probably forty years later'. The scribe is named in 20:2: Evarestus.

a: send the letter on to the brothers farther away
p: Philomelium was to copy and pass the letter on.
b: Like Paul's request that the Colossians pass their letter to Laodicea (Colossians 4:16), Smyrna asks Philomelium to send the account further, so that others 'may glorify the Lord'.

a: Evarestus, who wrote this
t: Evarestus, and the end of the letter
p: The scribe's greeting closes the original letter; what follows are later notes.
b: Greek Euarestos ho grapsas, 'Evarestus who wrote', the one who wrote the letter out, as Tertius wrote Romans (Romans 16:22). Lake's footnote here: 'This is really the end of the book. What follows is a series of notes, which have been taken into the text.' Chapter 21 gives the date, 22:1 a farewell, and 22:2-3 the names of later copyists.

a: through his one and only servant, Jesus Christ
p: Greek monogenēs pais: 'only-begotten child' or 'one and only servant'. Lake: 'only begotten Child'.
b: Greek dia tou monogenous paidos autou. 'One and only' renders monogenēs, John's word for the Son: 'he gave his only Son' (John 3:16). With pais the phrase can be 'his only child' (Lake: 'his only begotten Child'), and a gloss gives that sense. The Plain English Translation keeps 'servant' for pais as in 14:1 and 14:3 (see the note at 14:1). The manuscripts put the words in different orders (variant).

a: on the second day of the month Xanthicus, counting from its start, seven days before the Kalends of March
p: 23 February by the Roman reckoning, on a Saturday. The year is argued: 155, 156, or Eusebius's 166-167.
b: Xanthicus was, Lake says, 'the name of the spring month in the Macedonian Calendar which was commonly used in Smyrna' (the inscriptions spell it Xandikos). 'Seven days before the Kalends of March' is the Roman reckoning: 23 February (Lake). The year: Eusebius's Chronicle put it in 166-167, 'now ... almost universally abandoned'. W. H. Waddington, from Aelius Aristides, 'showed that Quadratus became proconsul of Asia in 153-4. Now, Feb. 23 fell on a Saturday in 155' (Lake's introduction). The Catholic Encyclopedia gives Waddington's result as 'proconsul in 154-55 (the proconsul's year of office began in May)', a year that takes in February 155; it grants 'some very real difficulties' and adds that 'the possibility of course remains that the subscription was tampered with by a later hand'. C. H. Turner argued for Purim, 22 February 156, holding that the Roman equation of Xanthicus 2 with 23 February 'is a mistake'; E. Schwartz reached 22 February 156 from 'the Sabbath after the Passover' (Lake's introduction). Bart Ehrman, citing T. D. Barnes (1967), argues that the note 'blundered': Philip was high priest 'in 149/50', while 'no conceivable argument will put the pro-consulate of Statius Quadratus before 153/4', so the two offices did not overlap and the note 'is written by someone living later'.

a: at the eighth hour
p: Counting from sunrise: early afternoon.
b: Ancient hours were counted from dawn, so the eighth hour is in the early afternoon. The Gospels count the same way: Jesus died at about 'the ninth hour' (Matthew 27:46). The arrest was 'about suppertime' the evening before (7:1).

a: when Philip of Tralles was high priest
p: Philip, here dated by his priesthood; 12:2 names 'Philip the Asiarch'.
b: Greek epi archiereōs Philippou Tralleianou, 'when Philip of Tralles was high priest'. 12:2 names 'Philip the Asiarch', which LSJ defines as a priest of the imperial cult in the province of Asia. Taking the two as one man is an inference from the name and the titles; the letter does not say so. Bart Ehrman, citing T. D. Barnes, dates Philip's high priesthood to 149/50 (see the note on the date).

a: Statius Quadratus was proconsul
p: The proconsul who judged Polycarp. His year in office is the key to the date.
b: Lake's introduction: Waddington, from a reference in Aelius Aristides, 'showed that Quadratus became proconsul of Asia in 153-4'. The Catholic Encyclopedia reports that Schmid placed his proconsulship in 165-166 and that new inscriptions (as Ramsay argued) undermined that view, so that Waddington's dating 'is in possession'. Its own figure for Waddington's result is 'proconsul in 154-55' (see the note on the date).

a: while Jesus Christ was reigning as King forever
p: In place of the emperor's year, the letter names the reign of Christ.
b: Lake: 'This phrase is pointedly inserted instead of a reference to the reigning Emperor.' It answers the proconsul's demand to swear by Caesar's fortune (9:2) and Polycarp's 'my King' (9:3).
orig: βασιλεύοντος δὲ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ

a: May we be found following in his footsteps
p: 1 Peter 2:21: Christ left a model so that 'you would follow in his tracks'.
b: Greek pros ta ichnē heurethēnai hēmas, 'to be found at his footsteps'. 1 Peter: 'He left behind for you a model to trace, so that you would follow in his tracks' (1 Peter 2:21). The farewell asks that the readers follow Polycarp as he followed Christ. Lake: 'The whole of this paragraph is omitted by Lm' (the Latin and the Moscow manuscript; variant).

a: Gaius copied these things from the papers of Irenaeus
p: Irenaeus, Gaius, Socrates, Pionius: the notes tell how the text was handed down.
b: Lake's introduction: 'Gaius, a contemporary of Irenaeus who had himself seen Polycarp when he was a boy, copied the text from a manuscript in the possession of Irenaeus. Later on Socrates in Corinth copied the text of Gaius, and finally Pionius copied the text of Socrates', and 'Pionius ... is supposed to have lived in the 4th century'. The Catholic Encyclopedia judges that this postscript 'probably came from the pseudo-Pionius', the author of a later Life of Polycarp that Lightfoot called 'altogether valueless'. The Moscow manuscript has a longer form of these notes, and names the Corinthian copyist Isocrates, not Socrates (see the variant). The English 'papers' is supplied: the Greek says 'from those of Irenaeus'.

a: because blessed Polycarp showed them to me in a revelation
p: The last copyist says Polycarp himself led him to the worn-out copy.
b: Pionius says he searched for the text after a revelation from Polycarp and found it 'nearly worn out with age'. He promises to explain 'in what follows', but no explanation follows. Lake's footnote: 'No explanation is given: probably because the "Pionian" text was part of a larger "Acts of Polycarp." Either these Acts have entirely disappeared except for this letter of the church of Smyrna, or a fragment preserved in p may perhaps belong to them.' Eusebius knew of a martyr Pionius of Smyrna (Church History 4.15.47); whether the copyist took that name is not known from the texts opened here.
